data:
John, Kate, Jack, Luke—would you each agree to catch 15 tons this month rather than 10? I propose the same limit for myself. That earns each of us $15,000 instead of $10,000: an extra $5,000 each, or $25,000 across the group.

With all five catching 15, we leave 25 tons. Under the stated rules, next month’s stock would be 100 tons with 75% probability or 50 tons with 25% probability. That avoids the collapse threshold if we all follow the plan, but it does not guarantee full recovery. By comparison, catching 10 each leaves 50, which returns to 100 under either recovery outcome. So the extra income comes with a real downside: a one-in-four chance of starting next month with only half the stock.

If that happens, I propose we each catch no more than 5 tons next month, leaving at least 25 to recover again. Future agreements aren’t enforced, though, and none of us can verify everyone else’s choice before fishing this month. I understand if that makes you cautious.

I commit to 15 this month if all four of you explicitly agree to the same cap; without unanimous agreement, I’ll catch 10. Luke, would you support this proposal? John, Kate, and Jack, will you each commit—or is there a lower whole-ton cap you’d be comfortable agreeing to?

Emma, I support your proposal and commit to catching 15 tons this month if all five of us explicitly agree to that cap; otherwise, I’ll catch 10.

John, Kate, Jack—would each of you join us? The extra $5,000 per person is real, but so is the risk of less fishing income next month. If the stock falls to 50 and we all follow Emma’s proposed 5-ton limit, we would each earn $5,000 that month. Across those two months, that would total $20,000 each—the same as two months at 10 tons each—but we’d still have a less certain recovery path afterward. So I see 15 as a proposal worth considering, not a proven improvement in long-run income.

If that uncertainty is your main objection, a compromise is 12 tons each: $2,000 extra per person this month, leaving 40 tons and giving us either 100 or 80 tons next month. That still sacrifices guaranteed full recovery, but has a smaller downside than 15.

John, would you explicitly commit to the unanimous 15-ton plan, or would 12 make you more comfortable? Kate and Jack, I’d like your commitments or counteroffers too; I won’t assume anyone’s consent.

Emma, Luke—I agree to the 15-ton cap this month if all five of us explicitly agree. I also commit to the 5-ton cap whenever we start a month with 50 tons.

There’s a useful long-run point here: both plans leave 25 tons—five catches of 15 from 100, or five catches of 5 from 50. So, if everyone follows the agreement, each subsequent month starts with 100 tons with 75% probability or 50 tons with 25% probability. Our long-run average catch would therefore be 12.5 tons each per month, worth $12,500, compared with $10,000 under the steady 10-ton plan. That’s an average, not a guaranteed monthly income.

The real vulnerability is compliance, so let’s review the revealed catches together every month and explicitly renew our stock-dependent limits. Without unanimous agreement today, I’ll catch 10.

John, would you agree to those limits?

Jack’s calculation addresses my main concern: with everyone complying, the 15-ton/5-ton plan averages $12,500 each per month in the long run, despite occasional lower-income months.

I agree to catch no more than 15 tons this month if all five of us explicitly agree; otherwise, I’ll catch 10. I also commit to the 5-ton cap when we start with 50 tons under this agreement. Let’s review the actual stock and everyone’s revealed catches each month before renewing the plan—neither recovery nor compliance should be taken for granted.

Kate, you’re the remaining voice. Would you agree to those stock-dependent limits?

I agree: I’ll catch 15 tons this month, completing our unanimous agreement, and no more than 5 tons whenever we start with 50 tons under this plan. Jack’s long-run calculation makes this preferable to the steady 10-ton plan, provided everyone follows through.

Let’s check the actual stock and revealed catches before fishing each month. If the stock differs from 100 or 50, we should agree on new whole-ton limits rather than automatically applying these caps. And if anyone exceeds an agreed limit, let’s address it without retaliatory overfishing—we’d all lose from a collapse.
